title: Jamestown founded
t: English colonists establish the first permanent English settlement in North America, in Virginia.

title: First enslaved Africans in English Virginia
t: About twenty Africans, taken from a Portuguese slave ship, are sold at Point Comfort, Virginia.

title: Plymouth Colony
t: The Mayflower lands Separatist Puritans and other English settlers in Massachusetts.

title: New Netherland
t: The Dutch West India Company begins settling the Hudson Valley; New Amsterdam follows in 1625.

title: Great Migration of Puritans
t: Roughly 20,000 English Puritans settle Massachusetts Bay over the next decade.

title: New Sweden
t: Swedish and Finnish colonists settle along the Delaware River.

title: England takes New Netherland
t: New Amsterdam becomes New York; the Dutch population remains.

title: Germantown founded
t: German Mennonites and Quakers settle near Philadelphia, opening Pennsylvania to German-speaking migration.

title: Ulster migration begins
t: Large-scale emigration of Presbyterian Scots-Irish from Ulster to Pennsylvania and the backcountry starts around 1717–1718.

title: New Orleans founded
t: French Louisiana's capital becomes the main entry point for enslaved Africans to the Gulf Coast.

title: Seven Years' War
t: War in North America and Europe sharply reduces transatlantic migration until 1763.

title: American Revolution
t: War halts most immigration and the slave trade until the 1780s.

title: Naturalization Act
t: Congress limits naturalization to "free white persons" of good character.

title: Louisiana Purchase
t: The US buys French Louisiana. South Carolina had reopened its slave trade in 1803, and imports surge until 1807.

title: Slave importation banned
t: The federal ban on importing enslaved people takes effect on January 1, 1808. Smuggling continues on a small scale.

title: Steerage Act
t: The first federal law regulating passenger ships requires arrival manifests, the basis of US immigration statistics from 1820.

title: Irish Famine
t: Potato blight causes famine in Ireland (1845–1852); over a million Irish emigrate to the US over the following decade.

title: Revolutions in Europe; Mexican Cession
t: Failed revolutions push German emigration. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transfers northern Mexico to the US.

title: California Gold Rush
t: Migrants arrive from China, Mexico, Chile, Europe and Australia.

title: Homestead Act
t: Free land in the West attracts Scandinavian, German and Czech farmers.

title: Page Act
t: The first restrictive federal immigration law, aimed mainly at Chinese women.

title: Chinese Exclusion Act
t: Chinese laborers are barred from entering; the ban is extended until 1943.

title: Ellis Island opens
t: The federal immigration station in New York Harbor processes most arrivals for the next three decades.

title: Peak year of the great wave
t: About 1.3 million immigrants are admitted, mostly from Southern and Eastern Europe. The Gentlemen's Agreement (1907–1908) limits Japanese labor migration.

title: World War I
t: War in Europe cuts transatlantic migration sharply.

title: Immigration Act of 1917
t: Adds a literacy test and an "Asiatic Barred Zone".

title: Emergency Quota Act
t: First numerical quotas by national origin, set at 3% of each group's 1910 population.

title: Johnson–Reed Act
t: National-origins quotas cut immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe and bar most Asians. The Western Hemisphere stays outside the quotas.

title: Great Depression
t: Immigration falls to its lowest level since the 1830s; hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and Mexican Americans are pushed to leave.

title: Bracero Program
t: A US–Mexico agreement brings Mexican contract workers (1942–1964); braceros were temporary workers, not counted as immigrants.

title: Chinese exclusion repealed
t: The Magnuson Act ends exclusion but sets a quota of 105 Chinese immigrants a year.

title: Displaced Persons Act
t: Admits about 400,000 Europeans displaced by World War II by 1952.

title: McCarran–Walter Act
t: Keeps national-origins quotas but ends the racial bar on naturalization.

title: Cuban Revolution
t: The first of several waves of Cuban exiles arrives in Florida.

title: Hart–Celler Act
t: Abolishes national-origins quotas in favor of family and skills preferences. Asian and Latin American immigration grows sharply.

title: Fall of Saigon
t: Refugee resettlement from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia begins.

title: Refugee Act; Mariel boatlift
t: Congress creates the modern refugee system. About 125,000 Cubans arrive by boat from Mariel.

title: IRCA amnesty
t: About 2.7 million unauthorized residents gain legal status. Most of them are counted as new permanent residents in 1989–1991, which produces the spike in those years.

title: Immigration Act of 1990
t: Raises overall limits and creates the diversity visa lottery.

title: September 11 attacks
t: Security reforms follow and the Department of Homeland Security takes over immigration services (2003).

title: COVID-19 pandemic
t: Consular closures and travel restrictions sharply cut new permanent residents in 2020 and 2021.
